title: Routing Protocols
summary: Distance-vector, link-state, hybrid, and path-vector protocols; administrative distance; metrics; RIP versions; loops; and static vs dynamic routing.

rows: Passes its routing table to neighbors. No full topology map.
Learns every link and builds the same topology map, then runs Dijkstra.
Routes between autonomous systems, tracking the AS path.

blocks.text: RIP has no topology table. It only trusts what its neighbors tell it.
AD ranks how much the router trusts each route source. When two sources offer the same route, the lowest AD is installed. Metrics only break ties between routes from the same protocol.
A static default route (AD 1) beats a RIP default route (AD 120), even if RIP has a lower metric.

items: RIP uses hop count. 1 to 15 is usable, and 16 or more is unreachable.
OSPF uses cost: reference bandwidth (100 Mbps) divided by interface bandwidth. Faster links cost less.
EIGRP uses a composite metric of delay, bandwidth, reliability, and load, weighted by K values.

blocks.text: RIPv2 multicasts. It does not broadcast.
A routing loop sends packets around a set of routers without ever reaching the destination. Each hop lowers the TTL, and the packet is dropped when TTL reaches 0.
Reaching TTL expiry is a symptom of a loop. The loop itself is packets circulating between routers and never arriving.

items: Dynamic routing reroutes around failures with no administrator action.
Static routing is typed in by an administrator and stays until someone changes it.
Default routes also need an administrator to change them if they fail.
Dynamic routing costs more RAM, CPU, and bandwidth, but it gives resiliency.
NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) discovers neighboring devices on IPv6 networks.
Router advertisements (RA) announce the gateway so hosts can find it.
Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 side by side.
Tunneling carries IPv6 inside IPv4. Teredo and ISATAP are tunneling methods.

title: Switching and Virtual LANs
summary: Switch learning and forwarding, VLANs, access and trunk ports, 802.1Q tagging, Spanning Tree, port security, QoS, and PoE.

items: Switches give the lowest latency and highest bandwidth. They use ASICs (application-specific integrated circuits) to forward frames in hardware.
A hub is a multiport repeater. It sends every signal to every port and shares the bandwidth.
A bridge is a software-based switch with higher latency than a switch.
Routers add latency because each packet is decapsulated, routed, and re-encapsulated.

sections.title: How a switch learns and forwards

items: A switch learns MAC addresses from the source MAC address of incoming frames, and stores them in its MAC address table.
It forwards each frame based on the destination MAC address in the table.
If the destination MAC address is not in the table, the switch floods the frame to all ports in the same VLAN.
Broadcast frames stay inside the VLAN they start in, because they cannot cross a router.

blocks.text: Switches learn from the source MAC address, not the destination. The destination decides where the frame goes.

items: Adding a VLAN increases the number of broadcast domains. It also increases the number of collision domains.
All switch ports start in VLAN 1 from the factory. VLANs 1 and 1002 to 1005 are protected by IOS and cannot be deleted.
Static VLANs are configured manually on each port. The node does not know which VLAN it is in.
Dynamic VLANs assign a port based on the device's MAC address, using a VMPS (VLAN Membership Policy Server). They are deprecated, and 802.1X is the recommended replacement.
Converting a flat layer 2 network to routed VLANs makes design more flexible but adds complexity to operations.

items: Hosts usually connect to access links.
Native VLAN traffic is untagged on the trunk. It is often used for management traffic between switches before both sides are configured as trunks.
Port security should be set on an access port. A trunk carries many MAC addresses, so port security does not work well there.
802.1Q is the open-standard trunking protocol. ISL is Cisco-only, so it cannot be used between switches from different vendors.
802.1Q inserts a 4-byte (32-bit) tag between the source MAC address and the type field.
The tag holds a 16-bit TPID of 0x8100, a 3-bit CoS field, a 1-bit drop-eligible indicator, and a 12-bit VLAN ID.

blocks.text: Tagged traffic is not placed on the native VLAN. Only untagged traffic is.

items: STP (802.1D) prevents loops in switched networks. RSTP (802.1w) is the faster version.
The root bridge is the switch with the lowest priority. If every priority is at the default, the lowest MAC address wins.
The default state for an STP port is blocking.
It takes 50 seconds for STP to converge from blocking to forwarding.
A routed, VLAN-enabled network is more flexible for user management and design than a flat layer 2 network, although operations get more complex.
To segment a workgroup such as R&D, create a new VLAN, configure a routed SVI (switched virtual interface), and apply ACLs to the VLAN interface.
ACLs belong on the VLAN (layer 3) interface. Extended ACLs cannot be applied to layer 2 switch ports.
Placing a new server in the new VLAN, or trunking the file server to both VLANs, does not restrict access.

blocks.text: Port security limits a switch port to a set number of MAC addresses. The addresses can be configured in advance or learned dynamically. It is set on an access port in access mode. It does not use jumbo frames or 802.1X, which control frame size and user authentication instead.

items: CoS is the layer 2 QoS method. It is a 3-bit field in the 802.1Q tag that maps to eight queues.
ToS and DiffServ are layer 3 QoS methods.
802.3at delivers 25.5 watts of power over Ethernet (PoE).

blocks.text: VTP (VLAN Trunking Protocol) propagates the VLAN database from a master copy on a server switch to client switches. It does not negotiate trunks or handle trunk encapsulation.

title: Introduction to IP Routing
summary: The IP routing process, frames versus packets, MAC addresses and ARP, reading a route table, static and dynamic routing, autonomous systems, and route selection.

items: A router decides where to send a packet using its route table and the destination network of the packet. It does not need the destination host, the originating network, or the return path to route the packet.
The frame changes at each hop. The packet is never changed until it reaches the destination host.
A frame carries a packet to only two places: a host on the local network, or a router interface when the packet is going to a remote network.
When the destination is on another network, the host sets the destination MAC address to the default gateway. The destination IP address never changes.

blocks.text: Frames are local and rebuilt at every hop. The packet, with its source and destination IP addresses, travels unchanged from the source host to the destination host.

items: MAC (hardware) addresses are always local. They are used only on the local LAN and never pass a router interface.
Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) finds the MAC address of the default gateway, or of a local host, from an IP address.
A host ARPs for the destination if it is on the same network. If not, it ARPs for the default gateway.
At the far end, the router interface facing the destination network ARPs for the destination host.
Reverse ARP (RARP) does the opposite, deriving an IP address from a MAC address, similar to DHCP. It does not update route tables.

rows: View the ARP cache on a Windows or Mac host
View the ARP cache on a Cisco router or switch
View the route table on a Cisco router

blocks.text: The chapter text prints arp -g in Exercise 9.1 and in question 6, but the command on a host is arp -a (question 18). Cisco routers use show ip arp.

items: The route table is the router's map of the internetwork. Routing decisions are made by destination network, not by host.
A C in the table means the network is directly connected because it is configured on an interface. An S is a static route.
The gateway of last resort is the default route. If it is not set and no route matches, the packet is dropped.
To find the exit interface, match the destination IP address to the network that contains it. 172.16.20.94 falls inside 172.16.20.64/27, so the exit interface is FastEthernet 0/2 (question 14).

blocks.text: A router with these four routes has no match for 172.16.20.100. That address sits between the /27 blocks, so the packet is dropped.

rows: The next device on this local network. For a remote destination, the default gateway.
The sender on this local network. Rewritten at every router hop.
Identifies the protocol inside the frame. 0x0800 is IPv4 and 0x0806 is ARP.
The IP packet. Unchanged by routers until it reaches the destination host.
A 4-byte cyclic redundancy check at the end of the frame. The destination uses it to verify the frame arrived intact.

blocks.text: The source MAC, destination MAC, and EtherType are included when the FCS is calculated, but only the FCS tells the receiver that the frame is intact.

items: If the router has no route to the destination network, it drops the packet.
The router also sends an ICMP destination unreachable message to the sender. The original packet is never returned.
Logging happens only if it is configured. Routers do not ask for dynamic updates when they meet an unknown network.
If a ping is lost along the way, the sender sees Request timed out. Destination unreachable appears when a router lacks the route.

items: The main job of a routing protocol is to update routing tables.
Convergence is the term for the result of all routes being updated in the routing table through a dynamic routing protocol. Faster convergence is better.

blocks.text: If a question asks for routing that is automated as new locations are added, the answer is dynamic routing, not static routing, DHCP, or RARP.

items: An autonomous system (AS) is a collection of networks or subnets in the same administrative domain.
An interior gateway protocol (IGP) is a dynamic routing protocol used inside an autonomous system. RIP, EIGRP, and OSPF are IGPs.
An exterior gateway protocol (EGP) is a dynamic routing protocol used between autonomous systems. BGP is the EGP in use today.
Administrative distance (AD) decides the most trusted route when two or more routes to the same network exist.
Distance-vector and link-state describe how routing protocols share and calculate routes. Chapter 10 covers them in detail.
Exam objective 2.1 lists three factors for route selection: prefix length, administrative distance, and metric.
A router first prefers the route with the longest matching prefix, because it is the most specific.
If prefix lengths tie, the router prefers the lowest administrative distance.
If administrative distance also ties, the router prefers the lowest metric.
